b: Share of voice measures how visible your brand is compared to competitors across social media, search, paid ads, and earned media.
The core formula is simple: your brand mentions divided by total industry mentions, expressed as a percentage.
Brands whose share of voice exceeds their market share tend to grow over time, which makes share of voice a leading indicator rather than a vanity metric.

Measuring share of voice is only half the job. Growing it comes down to consistent posting, conversation-worthy content, fast responses, smart budget decisions, and employee advocacy.
Share of voice is a way of measuring your brand’s visibility compared to your competitors. It’s a great metric to focus on if you’re looking to increase brand awareness or sales.
This pie chart shows how share of voice splits among four competitors.

In the past, share of voice was used to measure the success of your paid advertising. Now the definition covers overall online visibility: social media mentions, news and blog coverage, where you show up in organic search, and how often your ads appear.

It’s also more than a visibility score. Research from Les Binet and Peter Field, published by the IPA in The Long and the Short of It, popularised the idea of “excess share of voice,” which holds that when a brand’s share of voice is higher than its share of market, the brand tends to gain market share over time.
The reverse is also true. That relationship is why marketing leaders treat share of voice as an early signal of where the business is heading, not just a snapshot of who is loudest.
In short: share of voice tells you what percentage of the total conversation in your category belongs to you.

What about social share of voice?

Social share of voice is a way to measure how much people are talking about your brand on social media. It’s usually measured as a percentage of total mentions within an industry or among a defined group of competitors.

In other words, traditional share of voice tracks what brands say about themselves, and social share of voice tracks what people say about brands. You can also think of it as when social listening meets competitive analysis.

For example, if your brand sells running shoes, you should expect to show up in conversations about running, running shoes, and sneakers. Share of voice will give you an idea of how often your brand comes up compared to other brands in the same space.
Understanding your social share of voice puts all of your other social media analytics into context.
What is the difference between share of voice and share of market?
Share of voice and share of market sound similar but measure different things.
Share of voice tracks attention: how much of the conversation, coverage, or ad space in your category belongs to you.
Share of market tracks money: what percentage of category sales or revenue you actually hold.

The useful part is the gap between them. Share of voice moves first, share of market follows. If your share of voice is well above your share of market, you’re building the kind of awareness that usually converts into sales later. If it’s below, competitors are buying attention you’ll likely have to win back at a higher cost.

Social, organic search, paid search, earned media
Track both together. Share of voice tells you whether your marketing is working; share of market tells you whether it paid off.
Why should you measure share of voice?
Tracking share of voice helps you understand how visible your brand really is, and a higher share usually travels alongside stronger brand awareness and sales. Here’s what measuring it gives you:
Competitive analysis: See how you stack up against rivals, not just against your own past performance
Budget and resource allocation: Put money where your visibility gap is widest
Campaign effectiveness: Benchmark before and after a launch to see if it landed
Customer engagement and sentiment: Understand not only how often you’re mentioned, but how people feel about you
How does share of voice provide competitive advantage?

Share of voice shows you how your business stacks up against rivals, and it helps you stay ahead. Social share of voice doesn’t just track what people say about your business. It tracks what people say about your competitors, too.

Real-time listening makes that useful rather than academic. If a competitor’s share spikes in a single week, you can usually trace it back to a specific launch, partnership, or PR moment, then decide whether to respond, counter-program, or leave it alone.
How does share of voice help with budget allocation?

Share of voice shows you where to put your budget and resources. Maybe your brand owns the conversation on LinkedIn but barely registers on TikTok. Tracking share of voice shows you exactly where those gaps sit, by platform and by topic.

From there, the spending decision gets easier. Channels where you’re already strong often need less paid support, while channels where competitors dominate may need creative investment, community management, or a different content format altogether.
How does share of voice measure campaign effectiveness?
Share of voice shows how well a campaign landed by tracking how your share of mentions moves. If your share increases after running a campaign, you likely hit the right mark with your audience.

Record your share of voice in the weeks before a campaign launches so you have a clean baseline, then compare it against the weeks after. That single comparison is often more persuasive to leadership than impression counts.
How does share of voice relate to customer engagement and sentiment?

Share of voice is a volume metric, so pair it with sentiment analysis to get the full picture. A high share built on complaints is a problem, not a win, and negative mentions reached 20.7% in Q1 2026, up from 15.6% two years earlier. Insights drawn from sentiment or topic analysis can help inform your brand’s voice, engagement plan, and content.

Tracking and measuring share of voice can also help you attribute value to social media efforts in terms of leads, customers, and conversions. That data is what you take into budget conversations when you need to secure spend or make the case for more resources.
How to calculate share of voice
The share of voice formula is the same no matter which channel you’re measuring. Only the inputs change.
Your brand mentions / total industry mentions x 100 = share of voice

Here’s a worked example. If your brand received 2,000 mentions last month and total mentions across you and your competitors came to 10,000, your share of voice is 20%. Swap “mentions” for impressions, clicks, ranking visibility, or article counts and the math holds.

Before you calculate anything, decide two things: which competitors count as your set, and which keywords define your category. A set that’s too broad will flatten your numbers; one that’s too narrow will flatter them. Keep both consistent so your month-over-month comparisons mean something.

If you’re calculating this for social, you can gather the data using Hootsuite’s listening tools. They pull mentions from a range of platforms, including X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and more.

Once you have a dataset of all industry mentions, try segmenting it to get unique insights. For instance, you could segment mentions by location to see how your brand stacks up against competitors in different regions.

You can also apply other demographic filters, such as gender, age, or occupation. This can help you see if you have a larger social share of voice among one particular group. Use those insights to tailor content where you’re behind.
Analyzing social share of voice by sentiment and topic is also important. Your brand may have a high social share of voice, but if people aren’t saying good things, you’ll want to address that.
How do you measure social media share of voice?

You measure social media share of voice by tracking everything people say about your brand and your competitors on social platforms. This metric shows how well you’re connecting with your audience and participating in the conversations that matter to them.
To set up social share of voice tracking:
List your brand name plus common misspellings, product names, and branded hashtags
Do the same for three to five direct competitors
Add the category keywords your buyers actually use, like “running shoes” or “project management software”
Set a consistent time window, usually monthly, and exclude your own owned posts so you’re measuring earned conversation
Layer in sentiment and topic filters once the baseline is stable

How do you measure share of voice for SEO?

Share of voice for SEO measures the visibility of your website in organic search results compared to your competitors. It’s calculated from your ranking positions weighted by the search volume and click-through potential of each keyword, which is why it’s a better read on search performance than average position alone.

To calculate it, you’ll need a list of relevant industry keywords. Focus on the terms your buyers search before they know which brand to pick, plus the keywords tied directly to your product or service. A tracked set of 100 to 300 commercially relevant keywords is usually enough to see real movement.

You can use share of voice tools like Ahrefs’ Rank Tracker to compare your website’s visibility on these keywords to that of your competitors. The Competitors tab will show you how often your website is shown in search engine results pages (SERPs) compared to your competition.
Read the trend line, not the daily number. If your SEO share of voice climbs while your organic traffic stays flat, the issue is usually titles and snippets rather than rankings.

How do you measure share of voice for PPC?

Share of voice for PPC is the percentage of times your ad is shown compared to all the times it could have been shown for the same keywords. Google calls this metric impression share, and it’s the closest thing paid search has to a share of voice number.

For example, a 50% impression share means your ad appeared half as often as it was eligible to appear. The missing half is usually lost to budget or to ad rank, and Google splits that out for you so you know which lever to pull.
If you want to find your paid advertising share of voice, go to your Google Ads account, open Campaigns, then choose Columns from the top of the table.
The Columns button sits at the top of the campaign table in Google Ads.

Choose Competitive metrics, then select the impression share columns you want to track. Search impression share, search lost impression share (budget), and search lost impression share (rank) are the three worth watching together.
The Competitive metrics tab lets you add the impression share columns to your report.

How do you measure share of voice for media?

Your media share of voice is the number of times your brand is mentioned across news websites and blogs. For example, if your brand is mentioned in 40 articles and total industry mentions come to 100 articles, you have a 40% share of voice for that period.

Social listening tools double as share of voice tools here. Weight your results by publication reach rather than treating every mention equally. Twenty mentions in trade press often matter more to a B2B brand than two hundred in aggregator blogs.

How to increase your share of voice on social media
Once you have a good understanding of how your brand stacks up, you can focus on improving. Six tactics do most of the work:
A tried and true way to earn your brand’s piece of the pie is to stay active on all your social media channels. Customers will be more likely to reach out and engage if they know someone is there.

A good first step is to create a social media content calendar. Many important dates have higher social traction, and you don’t want to miss out. Use the calendar to make sure you have content ready when you need it and don’t end up repeatedly posting the same thing.
As well, try to post at times when your audience is most active on each network. This will ensure your content gets the greatest reach and potential pick-up.
Accounts known for consistent, in-the-moment posting, like Merriam-Webster on X, show what reliability buys you: people start tagging the brand in conversations it didn’t even start.
Since social share of voice represents brand mentions, giving people a reason to talk is one of the fastest ways to move the number.

Taking a firm stand on a topic your audience cares about will reliably lift mentions. Nike’s partnership with Colin Kaepernick and Gillette’s #TheBestMenCanBe campaign are still the textbook examples, and both show the trade-off: a large share of voice gain alongside polarised sentiment. Decide which of those two numbers you’re optimising for before you publish.

Brands don’t have to go near controversy to spark conversation, though. Bell’s annual Let’s Talk campaign has positioned the telecommunications company as a leader in the mental health conversation for well over a decade, generating a predictable annual spike in mentions.

Simpler prompts work too. Question posts, polls, and open calls for ideas cost nothing and routinely out-perform polished brand announcements on reply volume. Fenty Beauty launched with 40 foundation shades, turning a product fact into an invitation for customers to talk about their own match. Asking your community what to build next tends to do the same.
Another good way to increase social share of voice is to post content that people will want to share. The more original or meme-worthy, the better.
Three formats do the heavy lifting right now:
Short-form video: A strong format for shares and re-posts across TikTok, Reels, and Shorts
Carousels: Strong on LinkedIn and Instagram for saves and sends, which extend reach quietly
Interactive posts: Polls, quizzes, and “pick one” formats invite a reply rather than a scroll

Brands with a distinctive voice, like Netflix’s regional accounts or No Name’s deliberately plain product posts, get shared because the content is recognisable without the logo. That recognisability is what turns one post into hundreds of mentions.
Joining conversations about your brand is a good way to build customer relationships and make them feel good about your company.

Showing empathy and a touch of humanity can also go a long way. A Harvard Business Review study of airline accounts on Twitter found that when a customer service agent added their name or initials in their first reply, a customer’s willingness to pay for a future flight on that airline increased by $14 compared to those who received an unsigned response.

Speed matters as much as tone, which is where AI-assisted replies help. Hootsuite’s inbox can draft suggested responses and route conversations to the right person, so a growing mention volume doesn’t turn into a growing backlog.
By tracking your social media share of voice, you’ll have a better idea of where to invest in sponsored content, partner with social influencers, or allocate more support resources.

For example, if your voice is thin on X but healthy on Instagram, that might mean setting up a dedicated X profile for support questions rather than pouring ad spend into a channel where nobody is talking about you yet.
Having an informed social media strategy will allow you to focus on growing your share of voice where you need it the most.

Remember: social share of voice is ultimately about tracking conversations, and conversations inspire conversions. Plus, not all conversations take place on social media. Many happen in DMs, private channels, and offline, where they can’t be counted. So don’t rely on social share of voice alone to determine your success against your competitors.
It’s also important to measure what people say against what people do. Track social share of voice alongside other metrics that matter to your business.

Employee advocacy is the quietest lever on this list and often the most effective. When your team shares company content from their own profiles, it reaches networks your brand account never touches. Employees hold roughly 10x more connections than a company page has followers, and the content arrives from a person rather than a logo.
To build a program that actually moves share of voice:
Give employees a ready-made library of posts, with suggested copy they can edit in their own words
Focus on the people closest to customers, like sales, support, and recruiting
Make sharing optional and easy, and set clear guidelines on what can and can’t be posted

Measure the lift by tracking mentions and reach attributed to employee shares, then compare it against your brand-only baseline, since personal profiles generate 63% higher engagement than company pages

How do you define share of voice?

Share of voice is a metric that measures your brand’s visibility compared to competitors across a given market or channel. It can be calculated from social mentions, media coverage, organic search visibility, or paid ad impressions, depending on what you’re measuring.
How do you calculate share of voice?

You calculate share of voice by dividing your brand’s mentions (or impressions, clicks, or rankings) by the total across all competitors, then multiplying by 100 to get a percentage. For example, 2,000 brand mentions out of 10,000 total industry mentions equals a 20% share of voice.
What does 50% share of voice mean?

A 50% share of voice means your brand accounts for half of all the visibility, mentions, or impressions in your market or competitive set. In paid search, it means your ads appeared half as often as they were eligible to appear.
How do you check share of voice?

You can check share of voice using social listening tools like Lumen in Hootsuite Social OS, SEO tools like Ahrefs Rank Tracker, or the impression share columns in Google Ads for paid search. Most teams combine two or three, since no single tool covers every channel.
What is the difference between share of voice and share of market?

The difference between share of voice and share of market is that share of voice measures brand visibility and conversation volume, while share of market measures the percentage of actual sales or revenue a brand holds in its category. Share of voice is a leading indicator and share of market is a lagging one, which is why tracking both together is more useful than tracking either alone.
What is a good share of voice percentage?

A good share of voice percentage depends on your industry and the size of your competitive set, but the more useful benchmark is your own share of market. If your share of voice sits above it, you’re generally positioned to grow.
How often should you measure share of voice?

You should measure share of voice monthly, with more frequent checks during campaigns, product launches, or competitive shifts. Monthly gives you enough volume to spot real trends without reacting to normal week-to-week noise.
Can share of voice predict market share growth?

Yes, share of voice can act as a predictor of market share growth. Research by Les Binet and Peter Field, published by the IPA, popularised the “excess share of voice” principle, which holds that brands with a share of voice higher than their share of market tend to gain market share over time.
What is the best tool for measuring share of voice?

The best tool for measuring share of voice depends on the channel. For social and earned media, a listening platform like Lumen tracks mentions, sentiment, and competitor comparisons in one place; for organic search, use a rank tracker; for paid, Google Ads reports impression share natively.
Does share of voice include paid media?

Yes, share of voice includes paid media, where it’s typically measured as impression share. That figure shows how often your ads appeared compared to the total impressions available for your keywords, along with how much you lost to budget versus ad rank.
